b: "I will give my all and try to bring the crown to Uzbekistan," says 20-year-old World Championship Challenger Javokhir Sindarov in Chess.com's documentary, which will be released on November 20, days before the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship. On November 24, the Uzbek number-one, who shocked the world with the highest score in modern Candidates tournament history, will play Indian World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju (also 20) in the youngest world championship match ever.

Part one of the documentary includes never-before-seen footage of Sindarov's roots, with scenes from his childhood and interviews with his family, coaches, friends, and national team members. The story begins with a boy who lost all eight games in his first tournament and follows his path to becoming a champion, days before his most difficult challenge yet. Part two, which will be released after the world championship match, will show scenes from his training camp.
You can watch the approximately 54-minute video below and keep reading for the highlights.

One of the first scenes shows Sindarov playing Counter-Strike with his second, GM Mukhiddin Madaminov. In addition to being world number-four in chess (at the time of writing), Sindarov rates himself as around 2100-level at Counter-Strike. And he shows interest in starting a streaming career with that game "maybe later in my life."
The young man is, unsurprisingly, competitive, but says it runs in his family—no matter the game. "When we are playing even some friendly games, we are playing like it's a World Cup Final!"
When we are playing even some friendly games, we are playing like it's a World Cup Final!
Sindarov and his second playing Counter-Strike.

Sindarov started learning chess at the age of four, and he tells the story of his first tournament. He lost all eight games he played, with a full-point bye in one round. At the award ceremony, he expected some sort of reward for his single point, but didn't receive it. We, of course, know what happened after that.

Attributing his work ethic to an Uzbek saying, he says his success is "99 percent hard work, 1 percent talent. Probably I worked a lot in my childhood and that's why I became a strong player." Sindarov, who became a grandmaster at 12 years, 10 months, and days, is the sixth youngest grandmaster in history. (Read more about those records.)

Uzbekistan's current number two, though he was number one for many years, GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov, is one of the many figures to speak about Sindarov's rise. He remembers an early game with Sindarov, after which he concluded, "The game itself showed his strength... I managed to draw the game, but at the time it was obvious that he will be one of the strongest guys in Uzbekistan."
At the time it was obvious that he will be one of the strongest guys in Uzbekistan.
Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Uzbek board one in the Olympiad.

The documentary goes into more depth about Sindarov's journey before and after the pandemic—the sacrifices his family made and the lessons he learned from his failures and success. He came out of the lockdown with renewed motivation, as he says, "I was very hungry, I wanted to win some tournaments, I wanted to show myself. For me, not for someone else, for myself, that I can do it."
I wanted to show myself. For me, not for someone else, for myself, that I can do it.

Some of Sindarov's closest family members and peers speak to Chess.com. We hear from his grandfather, brother, teacher, childhood chess coach, childhood friend, GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, and his current coach, IM Roman Vidonyak. Sindarov's brother, Islom, who founded the Sindarov Chess School—where students can hold the 2025 FIDE World Cup trophy—says, "I'm really glad that chess is growing in Uzbekistan, and I'm really glad that I'm a part of that also."
I'm really glad that chess is growing in Uzbekistan, and I'm really glad that I'm a part of that also.
Javokhir Sindarov's brother shows the elementary school.

His grandfather jokes—and this shows his serious dedication—"Just a moment ago, a foreign guest spoke to me. He said that I had given up my career as a judge and prospector to devote myself to Javokhir. I replied that, although I didn't know where he had heard that, it was indeed true! Today we are witnessing that I made the right decision."

His coach, Vidonyak, shares a number of stories and insights, but one of them is that he has a new nickname for the world championship challenger. "He has many nicknames, but I call him predator now because he's becoming more and more a hunter. But he was also sonny boy and TNT, but now predator."
He has many nicknames, but I call him predator now because he's becoming more and more a hunter.

The latter segment of the documentary focuses on the upcoming world championship, with interviewees sharing their hopes and expectations. Sindarov let us in on a prophetic moment Assaubayeva had two years ago.

In 2024, we are watching Ding against Gukesh. and Sara was sitting with me and she said, I don't know, my intuition says to me: after two years you will play this match. I was laughing at this moment... Thanks a lot for saying these words, but I cannot even think about this because I need to work a lot!

Assaubayeva, who started talking to Sindarov five years ago, says, "I think his biggest challenge was to believe in himself, and I always told him, You are a super talented person. I have never seen this talent before in a chess player."
You are a super talented person. I have never seen this talent before in a chess player.
She also says: "I think it's very good when you find the person who understands you well... I think we are lucky to have each other."

Vidonyak gives a conservative prediction for the match. "[Sindarov is] a favorite. but who knows? I think in most cases you're going to have a fairly even match even if somebody is favored beforehand."
I think in most cases you're going to have a fairly even match even if somebody is favored beforehand.

Abdusattorov said of the match: "It's also a great honor for me to have such a friend and such a compatriot. It's incredibly inspirational to watch him always, and I wish him a lot of success and I wish him to win the title."

When Carlsen defeated GM Viswanathan Anand in 2013 to become the 16th world champion, he famously jumped into a swimming pool in his regular clothes. His brother Islom references this moment and says, "If he wins and if there will be a swimming pool, I would like to just hug him and jump into the swimming pool, I guess. But he needs to win first!"
Madaminov says, "If Javokhir wins this title, with my whole heart, with my whole soul, I will be really happy for him."

Sindarov has the last word. "To all my Uzbek fans: I express my deepest gratitude for your support along this journey. In the fight for the world chess crown, I'll give my all and try to bring the crown to Uzbekistan."
